subject: A proof no human has read, and a warship that burned in port
summary: A machine-checked proof of a famous math problem, a burning Russian warship, a late crash in Las Vegas and a police database breach shared Sunday.

lead.head: A proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that only a program has read
text: A proof is not a proof until people can follow it, and this one is not there yet. Lean and Mathlib communities certified a very long machine-checked proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a problem open since the nineteenth century. Reports say the author works at Anthropic. Elon Musk's post about it was the one that traveled.

The certification means a proof checker accepted every step. It does not mean a mathematician has read the argument, and the proof is not yet published. The checker is strong evidence about correctness and weak evidence about understanding.
That gap is the story. If the claim holds, the bottleneck in mathematics moves from finding proofs to reading them.

notes.head: A Russian corvette burns at a Libyan port
notes.text: Video shows the Russian corvette Merkury on fire at the port of Benghazi, and it is reported destroyed by an explosion. Libyan authorities and Ukrainian-aligned accounts give different causes, and nothing in the record settles which is right. Treat the video as proof of the fire and the causes as claims.

notes.head: Verstappen wins in Las Vegas after Russell hits the wall
notes.text: Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix for Red Bull in a race with many lead changes. George Russell finished ninth for Mercedes after hitting the wall late. Russell says he took a high-risk move for the win. That is the usual price of going for it on a street circuit.

notes.head: The FBI is reported to be investigating a police database breach
notes.text: Reports say the FBI is looking into a breach of the National Crime Information Center, the system police use to check warrants and wanted people. What was taken, and by whom, is not known. Until that is clear, the size of the problem is a guess.

text: Two of the day's stories were about verification. A checker accepted a proof nobody has read, and a video shows a fire while the cause stays disputed.

My call is that the checked claim deserves more patience than the loud one. Machines can now confirm things faster than people can understand them, and the stories worth trusting are the ones where both have caught up.
